It was great to meet with Florida State Representative Adam Anderson to continue our work on the Genomic Answers for Children’s Health Act. I appreciate his leadership at the state level, and I'm proud that our federal legislation builds upon those efforts to help ensure children enrolled in Medicaid who are suspected of having a rare disease or genetic disorder have access to genomic sequencing - a groundbreaking diagnostic tool that has quickly become the standard of care. For far too many families, the search for answers can take years, involving countless medical appointments, unnecessary tests, emotional uncertainty, and significant financial hardship. My Genomic Answers for Children’s Health Act is an important step toward changing that. By expanding access to advanced genomic sequencing and research tools, we can help children receive earlier and more accurate diagnoses, connect them with targeted treatments sooner, and improve health outcomes for those living with rare, complex, and often undiagnosed medical conditions. Every child deserves the opportunity to receive the right diagnosis at the right time, and I look forward to continuing to work with Representative Anderson to advance policies that bring hope and better care to families facing these difficult challenges.

The Turner Job Corps Center in Albany is just one of over 120 centers located in every state in America, in Democratic- and Republican-represented districts. Not only do these centers help train people to achieve gainful employment, but their training is also tailored towards workforce development that local businesses need. It is a win-win situation. As co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Job Corps Caucus that I lead with Rep. Because we could not improve the bill on this and other fronts during the debate, I had to vote against it. Most people know about Rosa Parks and her courageous act of defiance that sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott and helped lead to a court ruling ending bus segregation in Montgomery. But fewer people know about Sarah Mae Flemming of Columbia, South Carolina. 72 years ago, Flemming was assaulted by a bus driver after she sat in a section reserved for white passengers. She fought back in court, and in a groundbreaking ruling, a federal appeals court ruled that bus segregation could no longer be justified under the doctrine of “separate but equal.” Flemming's victory helped pave the way for the legal challenge that ultimately ended bus segregation in Montgomery and across the South.

C001053.text: Terrorists. Cartels. Human traffickers. Drug smugglers. Each day, ICE and Border Patrol agents and officers confront these threats head-on to keep America safe. It’s exactly why I have consistently voted to comprehensively resource these law enforcement professionals as they carry out their security missions. While the far-left hoped to eradicate funding for critical operations and weaken our border security apparatus, House Republicans have made clear that we will continue to support those who defend our homeland and keep our communities safe. That's why we passed the Secure America Act today. However, while I do not regret the objective of our actions today, I am appalled by the complete failure of Senate Democrats that led us to this moment. Chuck Schumer and his radical caucus twice shut down the government, instigating chaos across the nation. Since then, they have continued to diminish Article I and forced the use of reconciliation. It’s wrong – and deliberately undermines the appropriations process. The Constitution entrusts Congress with the power of the purse. Yet, in great irony, the Senate has shown greater concern for protecting an internal rule than fulfilling its constitutional duty. The filibuster is nothing more than an institutional habit. It is neither mentioned nor sanctioned in our founding documents. I would remind my peers on the other side of the Rotunda that no chamber precedent is greater than the bedrock of our Republic. Members swear an oath to uphold the Constitution – not the filibuster. I thoroughly regret the erosion of Article I authority that Senate Democrats have instigated, and the price everyday Americans have been forced to pay as a result. I hope the months-long charade that led us to this moment serves as a reminder that no partisan fixation is worth shutting down the government, abandoning constitutional responsibilities, and forcing Congress into extraordinary measures simply to perform its most basic duties. I believe in the Constitution, the power of the purse, and completing the appropriations process. I also believe in keeping the homeland safe. The Senate may have abandoned proper governing, but I will not abandon those who stand watch over our borders and protect our communities. Our work, of course, doesn’t end here. As the Fiscal Year 2027 Appropriations markups near completion, I am reminded that governing is a choice. The work I do, the votes I cast, and the actions I take will always be guided by one principle: fulfilling our obligations to the American people

For 39 years, Governor Bill Anoatubby has led my tribe, the Chickasaw Nation, with remarkable vision, a strategic hand, and unwavering dedication. His leadership has transformed not only the trajectory of the Nation, but the lives of the Chickasaw people.   Economically, his tenure has been nothing short of historic and unprecedented. Through Governor Anoatubby’s steady leadership, the Chickasaw Nation did more than just achieve its goals of economic development and self-sufficiency – it surpassed them. Under his guidance, the tribe evolved from dependence on federal funding to one that is self-sufficient and prosperous on its own. Today, thanks to him, the Chickasaw Nation supports more than 22,000 jobs and contributes $3.7 billion annually to Oklahoma’s economy, including $1.2 billion in wages and benefits.   However, Governor Anoatubby’s impact cannot be measured by just economics. Throughout his lengthy tenure, he also placed a significant emphasis on preserving and sharing the precious heritage of the Chickasaw Nation. Through initiatives such as the Chickasaw Nation Division of Arts and Humanities and the Chickasaw Cultural Center, he ensured that our history, language, arts, and culture would continue to inspire future generations.   These achievements, on top of many others, make it unmistakably clear: Governor Bill Anoatubby is the most consequential Chickasaw Nation leader since the removal period. And his influence has extended past just the Chickasaw Nation. His leadership and impact are respected by every Oklahoman.   For nearly four decades, Governor Anoatubby has embodied true commitment to the Chickasaw people and Oklahoma. The powerful combination of his leadership, vision, and generosity has allowed all of us in our state to shape a brighter future for ourselves and all those touched by the results of his leadership. On a personal level, I am fortunate to call Governor Anoatubby a mentor and a trusted friend.   His retirement is an enormous loss for the Chickasaw Nation, all Indian Country, and the state of Oklahoma. However, he leaves the tribe stronger than he found it, as he hands it off to his very competent and bright son, Chris, the Lieutenant Governor. I have no doubt Chris will carry on his father’s legacy with wisdom, competence, and care, and I look forward to seeing everything the future holds for the Chickasaw Nation.   In conclusion, to Governor Anoatubby, congratulations on a truly remarkable career and a lifetime of service. Thank you for your leadership, your vision, your friendship, and the legacy you leave behind. I wish you, Janice, and your entire family the best as you enter this next chapter.

C001063.text: Today, I voted to pass the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act to help address rising housing costs and increase housing supply. I met with business leaders and elected officials from the United States and Mexico to discuss cross-border commerce, industry, investment, and ways to strengthen the binational economy. Thank you to Webb County Judge-elect Jerry Garza, Mexican Consul Juan Carlos Mendoza Sánchez, Dip. Santiago González of Nuevo León, and everyone who joined the discussion. As one of the nation’s busiest trade corridors, Laredo plays a critical role in keeping goods moving and supporting businesses throughout South Texas. At a surprise recognition arranged by Mr. Narciso Castro and the Knights of Columbus, my office presented Mr. Gonzalez with a Congressional Recognition and an American flag in honor of his service to our country and our community. My Outreach Coordinator Frida Figueroa attended on my behalf. Mr. Gonzalez served as an educator with LISD and UISD and retired from Lyndon B. Johnson High School as a counselor. I thank him for his service to our nation, his dedication to Laredo students, and the example he has set for our community.

I had the privilege of presenting Mrs. Estela Gallegos Perez with a Congressional Recognition and naming her Congresswoman for the Day in honor of her remarkable life and lasting contributions to our community. At 100 years old, Mrs. Perez continues to inspire those around her. From becoming a naturalized U.S. citizen and serving as an educator, to supporting students through scholarships and achieving her lifelong dream of walking across the graduation stage this year to receive her Diploma of Merit from Martin High School, her story is a powerful example of perseverance, resilience, and faith. It was an honor to celebrate her extraordinary legacy alongside her family and loved ones. Congratulations to Mrs. Gallegos Perez on this well-deserved recognition and thank you for the example you continue to set for future generations.

For many Alaskans, the impacts of the conflict with Iran won't end when a peace agreement is signed and the Strait of Hormuz reopens. Many of our rural towns and villages rely on diesel generation to keep their lights on, homes warm, and to power four-wheelers and skiffs for subsistence hunting and fishing. These communities already faced some of the highest energy costs in the country, but those prices have now risen even further—often to $10 a gallon or more—and have been locked in for months, sometimes longer, because they only receive fuel shipments once or twice a year when sea ice has receded. We have a responsibility to help. For the past decade, the Ocean Observatories Initiative has generated publicly available, real-time data that provides crucial insights into changing ecosystem conditions and extreme weather. Today we honor the life and legacy of Gilbert “Butch” Wallace, a devoted husband, father, grandfather, friend, and public servant whose impact on our community will be felt for generations. Butch is survived by his beloved wife of 48 years, Carolyn Wallace, their two daughters, Heather Wallace and Michelle Boone, and grandson Tyler Muller. Together they built a family grounded in faith, service, and love. The Wilson family always welcomed him as “Uncle Butch,” Attorney General Alan Wilson and Palmetto State Armory founder Julian Wilson were especially encouraged by “Uncle Butch.” A Florida native, Butch attended Florida State University where he earned a degree in Communications and Business. He went on to build a successful State Farm Agency, serving his community for 48 years. Through his work, he not only helped countless families and businesses, butalso, created jobs and contributed to the economic growth of our state. For more than 20 years, Butch has served as avalued member of my staff, where he touched the lives of countless South Carolinians, including my own. His wisdom and unwavering commitment to others made him an indispensable member of Team Wilson and a trusted friend of all those who worked alongside him. His dedication to service extended far beyond his professional life. He was deeply involved in his community serving as a Charter Member and President of the West Metro Rotary Club, President of the National Kidney Foundation of South Carolina, a member of the National Federation of Independent Business State Advisory Council, and a member of the Boy Scouts of America Indian Waters Council Board.   Additionally, in 2019, he was a recipient of the Order of the Palmetto, South Carolina’s highest civilian award. His commitment to civic engagement led him to serve in many political leadership roles including as Chairman of the Lexington County Republican Party and as a delegate to many state and county conventions. Butch lived a life defined by service, integrity, and kindness. South Carolina is better because of his contributions, and all who knew him are better for having called him a friend. He leaves behind a legacy of leadership, compassion, and service that will endure long beyond his lifetime. May we honor Butch by striving to serve others with the same dedication and grace that he demonstrated throughout his remarkable life.

F000466.text: RT by @RepBrianFitz: When both sides choose to work together, big things can get done. Tonight, the House passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act with overwhelming bipartisan support, advancing a bicameral effort to address one of the biggest challenges facing American families: housing affordability. Addressing our toughest challenges requires collaboration, and tonight’s vote is a strong example of what that can achieve.

Tonight, the House gave final approval to the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act with overwhelming bipartisan support, sending one of the most significant federal housing reform packages in years to the President’s desk. For families across our community, housing affordability is not an abstract policy debate. It is the young couple trying to buy a first home, the senior trying to downsize or stay in the community they helped build, the veteran navigating a mortgage, and the working family squeezed by a market that has not built enough homes, fast enough, for far too long. That is why I made housing a central pillar of the @ProbSolveCaucus Affordability Agenda that @RepTomSuozzi and I launched earlier this year. Over the past several months, I have sat down with realtors, builders, lenders, local officials, veterans, seniors, young families, and first-time homebuyers across our district to identify what is broken, where federal policy is getting in the way, and what Congress can do to help lower costs and expand supply. Tonight, that work is moving from idea to law. The final bill includes key housing reforms I helped advance to: ✅ Accelerate responsible homebuilding and cut costly delays ✅ Strengthen housing vouchers and expand landlord participation ✅ Ensure veterans and servicemembers know about the VA Home Loan benefits they earned ✅ Help veterans clearly compare VA Home Loan options when buying a home ✅ Turn vacant and underused properties into affordable homes ✅ Support housing investment and neighborhood revitalization This is a major affordability win— and exactly what our agenda was built to do: bring both parties together, turn practical solutions into law, and help put the American Dream back within reach for working families. 🔗 Read more: http://fitzpatrick.house.gov/2026/6/fitzpatrick-backed-housing-reforms-head-to-president-s-desk-marking-major-problem-solvers-caucus-affordability-win-for-pa-1-families

Seventy years ago today, Jim Fitzpatrick put on a white jacket and married Mary Margaret Williams. This past weekend, with my parents there beside us, I put on a white jacket and married my best friend. A tribute to the first love story I ever knew. My parents’ life together is one of those great American stories—built quietly, faithfully, and day by day by a U.S. Army soldier and a secretary who believed in faith, family, hard work, service, and each other. From that beginning in Levittown, where they remain today, came eight children, countless grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and a home full of life, faith, sacrifice, steadiness, and love. They have known joy and hardship, laughter and worry, triumph and loss. They have seen seasons change and the world around them transform. And through it all, they have remained what they have always been: steady, faithful, and together. My mother’s faith steadied our home and my father’s quiet strength anchored it. Together, they showed us that love is not simply the promise made at the altar. It is the promise kept after it. Kept in a marriage, through children and grandchildren, through joy and hardship, through faith, service, and sacrifice. That is the American Dream they built, and protected, for seventy years. Their marriage is not only something to celebrate. It is something to behold. Happy 70th Anniversary, Mom and Dad. Your love built our family, and your American Dream lives on in every life made possible by yours.

This morning at Historic Boone Farm in Middletown Township, on Juneteenth, our community witnessed something truly special: a dream realized. The African American Museum of Bucks County now has a home worthy of the history it preserves, the stories it carries, and the generations it will teach. On a day that reminds us freedom must be taught, protected, and remembered, this museum gives our community a permanent place to do that sacred work. This day belongs to my dear friend, the late Linda Salley. For years, Linda carried these stories across our community—into schools, churches, libraries, and gathering places—because she knew Bucks County’s African American history deserved to be known, honored, and passed on. She was right. Working alongside Linda and the AAMBC team to bring this vision to life has been one of the great honors of my service, including securing $2 million to help complete the restoration and expansion of Boone Farm. Linda and I shared a deep belief that this history deserved more than a temporary home. It deserved permanence. It deserved a place to stand. And today, because of her vision and the dedication of so many, it has one. The story of Bucks County cannot be fully told without the stories this museum preserves. And because of Linda’s faith, leadership, and love for this community, those stories will continue to teach, inspire, and endure for generations. Congratulations to the entire AAMBC team, board, staff, volunteers, partners, and every person who made this possible—and my sincere thanks to my incredible friend, Pastor Don Schuler, for providing such special remarks on my behalf.

On June 19, 1865, more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation, Union troops arrived in Galveston, Texas, to announce and enforce emancipation—a turning point in our nation’s long march toward justice. For those who had been denied the truth of their freedom, Juneteenth marked a long-overdue day of liberation. For our nation, it remains a defining moment in America’s ongoing journey toward justice, equality, and human dignity. That is why, in 2021, I helped lead the effort to establish Juneteenth as a federal holiday—to honor this historic moment, preserve its rightful place in our national memory, and recognize the generations of Americans whose courage, faith, perseverance, and sacrifice have carried our country closer to its founding ideals. As Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. reminded us, “Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.” Today, we honor this legacy by reflecting on that truth and renewing our commitment to justice, equality, freedom, and dignity for all.

O000172.text: RT by @RepAOC: Thunderstorms and the chance of flash flooding move into NYC today. Heavy rain, strong winds, hail, and lightning are all possible. High winds can knock down trees and power lines and send debris flying. Heavy rain can flood streets and basement apartments fast, often with very little warning. NYCEM activated the city's Flash Flood Emergency Plan on Thursday. We have been preparing since then and through the day, coordinating with agency partners and tracking conditions around the clock so the city is ready and New Yorkers get the word in time to act. Now we need you to do your part. Know your risk. If you live in a basement or ground-floor apartment, a low-lying neighborhood, or an area that has flooded before, you are at higher risk. Take a few minutes now to get ready. Before the storm: Sign up for alerts at http://nyc.gov/notifynyc or text NYC to 692-692. If you live in a basement apartment, select the basement apartment alert option so you get warnings that apply to where you live. Bring in or tie down anything that can blow away, like trash cans, lawn furniture, plant pots, and umbrellas. Clear debris from basement windows, stairwell drains, and gutters so water can flow. Make sure your basement exits are clear and easy to open. Keep a Go Bag near your door with medications, a flashlight, a phone charger, and important documents in waterproof bags. When it hits: If you hear thunder, head inside and move away from windows to an interior room on a lower floor. Do not touch electrical equipment or plumbing during a thunderstorm. If a Flash Flood Warning or Emergency is issued, act immediately and move to higher ground. Do not wait to see the water. Never walk or drive through floodwater. Just 6 inches can knock you off your feet, and 1 foot can sweep away a car. Once you leave a flooded area, do not go back until officials confirm it is clear. Flooding can develop overnight, so keep your phone nearby with alerts on and the volume up. Sign up at http://nyc.gov/notifynyc and get more storm and flooding tips at http://nyc.gov/beready.

From day one, the majority of Americans did not want this war. If President Trump had come to Congress, as the Constitution requires, we would have told him that. But this Administration pressed on anyway – despite the cost, despite the law, and despite the will of the people. Now, after billions of taxpayer dollars spent and 13 American servicemembers’ lives lost, we are no better off in Iran than we were before the war began. Iran’s nuclear ambitions have not been eliminated. Iran has more control over the Strait of Hormuz now than it did before this war, and more access to capital than before the war as well. Here at home, we have paid more at the gas pump and on other essentials as a result. We would be in the same position, if not better, had President Trump never torn up the JCPOA, President Obama’s 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran. This is what happens when you disregard the will of the people, ignore the work and lessons of those before you, and start a war before understanding and defining your objectives or strategy. This is what happens with President Trump and Secretary Hegseth at the helm. We cannot afford more of this irresponsible leadership.

President Trump is right — the Senate Parliamentarian needs to go.   I said the same thing last year after she struck down my amendment ending taxpayer funding for sex reassignment procedures.   The Parliamentarian’s job is not to decide whether a policy is good or bad. It’s to determine whether a provision complies with the Senate’s budget rules governing reconciliation.   My amendment directly controlled federal spending, thus it was within the budget rules. The Parliamentarian ruled it out of order anyway.   Republicans are always told these decisions are neutral and beyond question. But when the Parliamentarian consistently blocks conservative priorities, while Democrats face no such obstacles, it's fair to ask whether the rules are being applied fairly.   Bottomline: the Parliamentarian serves at the pleasure of the Senate Majority Leader, not for life. If Republicans want to enact the agenda voters sent them to Washington to deliver, they have every right to replace her with someone who will apply the rules consistently.

Yesterday, before watching the world’s best golfers compete at the U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills, Kaylie, Reagan, and I spent time with my friends from the Shinnecock Nation on their tribal land. Their story is one of faith, family, resilience, and perseverance, a story I grow to appreciate more with every visit. Vice Chairman Lance Gumbs gave us a personal tour of the Shinnecock Museum, the reservation, and the resting places of some of the Nation’s ancestors. As we focused on the headstones, I was struck by how many Shinnecocks had served in the U.S. military. Lance shared that Native Americans have long served at higher rates than the general population, a tradition that continues today. In fact, since 9/11, roughly 19% of Native Americans have served in the Armed Forces, compared to about 14% of Americans from other ethnic groups, a remarkable testament to their patriotism and commitment to service. After the tour, I met with Chairwoman Lisa Goree and the Council of Trustees at the Nation’s headquarters in Southampton. We talked about the nation’s 800 people, and what the council is doing to promote education, economic independence, and quality of life. For more than 13,000 years, the Shinnecock people have called this land home. As skilled whalers, artisans, and steadfast stewards of a rich Algonquian heritage, they have helped shape the history and character of the East End. Their enduring contributions, strength, and spirit are an important part of what makes hosting the 2026 U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills so meaningful.

B001323.text: I recently had the opportunity to visit the XPRIZE Wildfire competition at Nenana Airport alongside Cathy Cahill, Director of the Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration. It was impressive to see firsthand how innovators are developing autonomous technologies that can detect and respond to wildfires faster than ever before. As Alaska faces increasingly challenging wildfire seasons, early detection and rapid response can mean the difference between a small ignition and a devastating fire that threatens critical infrastructure, and natural resources. The recent wildfire activity near Anderson and Clear Space Force Station highlights exactly why these innovations matter. Investing in cutting-edge technology, strengthening our wildfire preparedness, and improving forest management must remain national priorities. That is why I am proud to co-sponsor the Fix Our Forests Act and support the work of the House Natural Resources Committee, which has made wildfire prevention and forest resilience a key priority this Congress. By combining responsible forest management with emerging technologies, we can reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfires and better support our first responders. Thank you to the teams competing in Alaska, Cathy Cahill and her team, and everyone working to advance solutions that will help keep Alaskans safe.

J000311.text: On this day in 1944, over 34,000 American soldiers crowded together in small, amphibious boats en route to Omaha Beach. As the boats landed on the beach, and their bow ramps dropped down leading the men ashore, unrelenting machine gun fire rained down from enemy bunkers. Undeterred, the American and Allied forces emerged from the battle victorious, but not without a heavy cost. Over 2,500 Americans died at Omaha Beach. One of them was 1st Lieutenant Thomas Royce Dallas Jr. from our Congressional District in Griffin, Georgia, who drew his last breath on the shores of Omaha Beach. As we remember the heroism Americans exhibited on D-Day and we reflect on the cost of freedom, may we remember and be inspired by the names and faces of those brave soldiers who died in service to our Country.

Today, we fully reopened the Tyrone Post Office! Before I was sworn into Congress, I promised to reopen the Tyrone Post Office, which had previously suffered extensive structural damage due to a fire.  As of today, the Tyrone Post Office is fully open for business. I spoke with @WTHRcom about my work to keep Hoosiers safe on our roads. Too many families have been hurt by preventable crashes involving unsafe drivers and trucking companies that should not have been operating in the first place. The SAFE Act is straightforward: if a trucking company racks up serious safety violations, it should not be able to shut down, reopen under a new name, and keep putting families at risk. We need stronger accountability for dangerous carriers and drivers who ignore the law.

With Alzheimer’s, time matters. The earlier families have answers, the earlier they can plan, pursue treatment, and make the decisions ahead of them with clarity. WORLD_GERMANY_CHANCELLOR.text: Wir kehren den Trend um: Die Rentenbeiträge sinken, das Versorgungsniveau steigt.  Wir machen Rentenpolitik nicht nur für eine Legislaturperiode. Wir machen Politik für die nächsten Generationen.

Die Empfehlungen der Alterssicherungskommission sind klug und klasse. Herzlichen Dank an Frau Professor Janda und Herr Weise sowie alle Mitglieder. Damit tragen wir auch zu Wachstum- und Beschäftigung bei – Deutschland und unserem Wirtschaftsstandort wird das gut tun.

Eine verpflichtende Kapitalrente macht das System stark. Sie verbessert die Versorgung im Alter und nutzt die guten Effekte des Kapitalmarktes. So können mehr Menschen am Wachstum unserer Volkswirtschaft teilhaben.

Die Rente bleibt sicher in der Zukunft und die Lasten dafür werden gerecht verteilt – über alle gesellschaftlichen Gruppen und Generationen. Ohne Reform würden das Rentenniveau sinken, die Beiträge steigen. Das kehren wir um.
Reformen sind kein Selbstzweck. Wir reformieren aus Notwendigkeit.

À chacun d’entre eux, j’ai rappelé l’engagement de la France en faveur de la souveraineté et de l’intégrité territoriale du Liban. La mise en place d’un cessez-le-feu robuste, qui doit être respecté par tous, doit permettre d’engager un processus simultané de retrait israélien du territoire libanais et de redéploiement des forces armées libanaises, afin de garantir l’exercice par l’État du monopole des armes. La France est prête à accompagner concrètement ce processus et à mobiliser la communauté internationale dans les prochaines semaines, aux côtés du gouvernement libanais, pour soutenir les forces armées libanaises et répondre aux besoins des populations déplacées.
